blocks.text: A shackle holds a 4 tonne engine block from a crane hook, and the whole load passes through one steel pin about the size of your thumb. Whether that pin shears, crushes the plate around it, or merely deforms elastically depends on three different stresses, each defined by force divided by a different area.

blocks.markdown: **Stress** is internal force per unit area. The simplest case is the **average normal stress** in an axially loaded member: if an axial force $P$ acts through the centroid of a prismatic bar of cross-sectional area $A$, and the section is away from the loaded ends, the stress is assumed uniform: $\sigma = P/A$. It is tensile (positive) when the bar is pulled and compressive (negative) when it is pushed. The SI unit is the pascal, and $1\ \text{N/mm}^2 = 1\ \text{MPa}$.

blocks.title: Normal, shear and bearing stress
blocks.text: Normal stress acts perpendicular to a surface; **shear stress** $\tau$ acts parallel to it (average value $\tau = V/A$, with $V$ the shear force on the section); **bearing stress** $\sigma_b$ is the contact pressure between two bodies (average value $\sigma_b = P/A_b$, with $A_b$ the projected contact area).

blocks.caption: $A_s$ = area of the shear plane(s) resisting; $d$ = pin diameter; $t$ = plate thickness.

blocks.title: Stress in a tension rod
blocks.prompt: A steel rod of diameter 16 mm carries an axial tensile force of 38 kN. Find the average normal stress.

steps.text: Cross-sectional area of a solid circle.
Use sigma = P/A with P in newtons and A in mm^2 to obtain MPa.

blocks.answer: The rod carries an average tensile stress of 189 MPa.

blocks.markdown: **Pins and bolts in shear.** A pin that joins two members is cut by the load across a plane where the members meet. In **single shear** the pin has one such plane, so the shear force on it is $V=P$. In **double shear** (a clevis, where a middle member is held between two outer ones) there are two planes and each carries $V = P/2$. The area per shear plane is $\pi d^2/4$ for a solid round pin.

blocks.title: Clevis pin in double shear
blocks.prompt: A clevis pin of diameter 12 mm carries a tie force of 40 kN with the tie held between the two arms of a clevis. Find the average shear stress, and compare it with the same pin in single shear.

steps.text: Two shear planes, so each shear force is half the load.
In single shear the whole 40 kN would act on one plane.

blocks.answer: Double shear gives 176.8 MPa, exactly half of the 353.7 MPa that single shear would give.

blocks.caption: Which force and which area for each stress

blocks.markdown: **Bearing.** The pin presses against the wall of the hole. The true contact pressure varies around the hole, so we use the **projected area**: pin diameter times plate thickness. A thick plate spreads the load over more area; a thin plate with a big pin load may be crushed or tear out even if the pin is strong enough in shear.

blocks.title: Bolt and plate in a lap joint
blocks.prompt: Two plates are joined by one 16 mm bolt in single shear and transmit a 30 kN tensile force. The thinner plate is 10 mm thick. Find the average shear stress in the bolt and the bearing stress on the plate.

steps.text: Single shear: V = 30 kN. Bolt area is 201.1 mm^2.
Bearing uses projected area d t = 16 x 10 = 160 mm^2.

blocks.answer: The bolt sees 149 MPa shear and the plate 187.5 MPa bearing; they are checked separately against their own allowable values.

blocks.title: Do not mix areas
blocks.text: Shear uses the area cut through the pin; bearing uses the projected area d x t. Using the circumference times thickness, or forgetting that double shear halves the force on each plane, are common errors. Average stress is valid only when the load acts through the centroid.

points: Average normal stress is sigma = P/A, with A perpendicular to the axial force.
Average shear stress is V/A_s; in double shear V = P/2 on each of two planes, in single shear V = P.
Bearing stress is P/(d t) using the projected contact area, and is checked separately from shear.

questions.stem: The diameter of a round rod loaded in axial tension is doubled while the force is kept the same. What happens to the average normal stress?

distractorRationale.a: Treats stress as inversely proportional to diameter instead of area.
distractorRationale.b: Stress depends on area, and area has changed.
distractorRationale.c: Correct: A scales with d squared, so stress falls by 4.
distractorRationale.d: Mixes with a cubic dependence such as section modulus.

questions.explanation: Area is proportional to d^2, so doubling d multiplies the area by 4. With the same force, sigma = P/A is divided by 4.

questions.stem: A pin transmits a force P through a clevis, with the central member between two outer arms, so that it is in double shear. What is the shear force acting on each pin cross-section?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: two planes share the force equally.
distractorRationale.c: The shear force cannot exceed the transmitted load.

questions.explanation: A pin in double shear is cut across two planes that act in parallel, so each carries half of the transmitted force, V = P/2. The shear stress is therefore half of the single-shear value for the same pin.

questions.stem: A 20 mm diameter pin passes through a plate of thickness 8 mm. What area should be used when computing the average bearing stress between pin and plate?

distractorRationale.a: This is the pin's cross-sectional area pi d^2/4, which is the shear area.
distractorRationale.b: This is the cylinder contact surface pi d t, not the projected area.
distractorRationale.c: Has no physical basis; confuses d^2 and thickness.
distractorRationale.d: Correct: projected area d x t = 20 x 8.

questions.explanation: Bearing stress uses the projected contact area, the pin diameter times plate thickness: 20 x 8 = 160 mm^2. The pin's own cross-section (314 mm^2) is the area for shear, not bearing.

questions.stem: Which condition is required for the average normal stress sigma = P/A to represent the actual stress at a section of a bar?

options.text: The bar is made of steel
The load acts through the centroid and the section is away from the loaded ends
The bar has a circular cross-section

questions.correctOptionText: The load acts through the centroid and the section is away from the loaded ends

distractorRationale.a: Material does not determine the stress distribution at equilibrium.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: uniform stress needs centroidal loading and distance from concentrations.
distractorRationale.d: Dynamic loading would change the loads, not the validity of the definition.

questions.explanation: Uniform distribution requires that the resultant of the stresses is the axial force, so the load must act through the centroid. Near points of load application the distribution is non-uniform (St Venant), so the formula applies away from them.

questions.stem: True or false: a bolt in single shear carries the full transmitted force P as the shear force on its one resisting plane.
questions.explanation: With one shear plane there is nothing to share the force, so V = P and tau = P/A. Double shear halves V because two planes resist.

questions.stem: An aluminium rod of diameter 10 mm carries a tensile force of 12 kN. Find the average normal stress in MPa.
A 20 mm diameter bolt joins a tie plate between two outer plates (double shear) and transmits 90 kN. Find the average shear stress in the bolt in MPa.
questions.explanation: Each of the two planes carries 45 kN and has area pi(20)^2/4 = 314.2 mm^2, so tau = 45 000/314.2 = 143.2 MPa.

questions.stem: A 20 mm pin transmits 45 kN to a bracket plate. The allowable average bearing stress of the plate material is 150 MPa. What minimum plate thickness is required, in mm?
questions.explanation: Bearing area needed = 45 000/150 = 300 mm^2. With d = 20 mm, t = 300/20 = 15 mm.

questions.stem: Explain the difference between single shear and double shear for a pin, and why a pin in double shear can carry roughly twice the load for the same allowable shear stress.
markingGuide: Defines single shear as one plane resisting the load and double shear as two planes
States V = P in single shear and V = P/2 per plane in double shear
Writes tau = V/A with A the pin cross-section
Concludes that for the same allowable tau, P allowed = tau A for single shear and 2 tau A for double shear
Mentions the clevis arrangement or a centre member between two outer plates as an example
questions.explanation: The number of shear planes determines how many pin areas share the load. Two planes double the resisting area for the same transmitted force.

questions.stem: A pin has adequate shear strength but a thin plate around the hole becomes permanently deformed. Explain what stress governs this and why the projected area is used for it.
markingGuide: Identifies bearing (contact) stress between pin and hole wall
Explains that the actual pressure varies around the hole, so d t is a projected-area average
Explains why a thinner plate increases sigma_b for a given load
Distinguishes bearing from shear stress in the pin, which uses the pin cross-section and a different allowable value
questions.explanation: The load is transferred through contact pressure on the hole surface, so bearing stress is a separate check from shear. Thinner plates have less projected area and therefore higher bearing stress.
